issues.legal_issue: A review may correct a self-evident error where a later legal change applies to a proceeding that had not reached finality and the change was not available for consideration in the original decision.
material_facts: The tenant’s application to purchase the land remained pending when the statutory amendment took effect.
The amendment and the resulting exemption for qualifying religious institutions had not been available when the earlier decisions were made.
The materials before the reviewing court showed that the landlord institution fell within the amended provision.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in allowing review because the intervening amendment made the earlier decision an apparent error in the circumstances, and the issue could be resolved from the record without a rehearing.
issues.legal_principle: Order XLVII Rule 1 CPC permits review for newly discovered important matter or evidence despite due diligence, mistake, error apparent on the face of the record, or another sufficient reason. An apparent error must be manifest and not one that must be found through further investigation; review is not a rehearing of the same issue. The Court applied the principles described in Kunhayammed v. State of Kerala concerning review after summary dismissal of a special leave petition.

rule.if: review_application and later_law_applies_to_pending_proceeding and later_law_was_unavailable_at_original_decision and record_makes_error_self_evident

predicates.review_application: A party sought review of an earlier court decision.
predicates.later_law_applies_to_pending_proceeding: A later legal change governs a proceeding that had not reached finality when the change took effect.
predicates.later_law_was_unavailable_at_original_de: The legal change had not been enacted or was otherwise unavailable for consideration when the original decision was made.
predicates.record_makes_error_self_evident: The materials already on the record make the error apparent without further investigation or a rehearing.

issues.definition: When a review application concerns a proceeding still pending under a later legal change that was unavailable at the original decision, review is permissible if the record makes the error self-evident.

issues.legal_issue: An organization shown by the evidence to be a place of public religious worship qualifies as a religious institution under the amended statutory definition.
material_facts: The organization produced documentary evidence and testimony about its activities.
The evidence showed that religious ceremonies, prayers, and masses were conducted there for people of the Christian faith, particularly those of the Roman Catholic denomination.
The High Court found that the organization came under a diocese whose objects included maintaining churches, and the trial court likewise found it to be a place of worship.
issues.conclusion: The organization was a religious institution within the meaning of the amended provision.
issues.legal_principle: Section 1(f) of the Madras City Tenants’ Protection Act, 1921, as amended by Tamil Nadu Act 2 of 1996, defines a religious institution to include a church or other place used as of right by a community or section of it as a place of public religious worship. The Court relied on the factual findings based on oral and documentary evidence.

predicates.tenant_land_purchase_dispute: The dispute concerns a tenant’s claimed right to purchase land from a landlord under a tenant-protection scheme.
predicates.evidence_shows_place_of_public_religious: Evidence shows that the entity is used by a community or section of it for public religious worship.

issues.definition: In a tenant land-purchase dispute, an entity shown by the evidence to be used for public religious worship qualifies as a religious institution.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s purchase proceeding does not end merely because the purchase price has been deposited or an order directing conveyance has been made; it ends when the conveyance is executed.
material_facts: The tenant had deposited the full site value and obtained an order directing the landlord to convey the land.
The sale deed had not been executed when the statutory amendment took effect.
The sale deed was executed only after the amendment had taken effect.
issues.conclusion: The proceeding remained pending until execution of the sale deed, so the tenant could not rely on the proviso protecting proceedings already fully executed or satisfied before the amendment took effect.
issues.legal_principle: Section 9(3)(a) and (b) of the Madras City Tenants’ Protection Act, 1921, requires an order directing conveyance and provides for dismissal of the suit or proceeding, but the Court held that the proceeding remains pending until a proper document conveys title. The Court rejected the contrary view in Arulmigu Kasi Viswanathaswamy Devasthanam v. Kasthuriammal because it conflicted with the statutory language.

predicates.tenant_land_purchase_proceeding: A tenant is pursuing a proceeding to purchase land from the landlord under a statutory purchase right.
predicates.purchase_price_deposited: The tenant has deposited the price fixed for the land.
predicates.conveyance_not_executed: No conveyance transferring title to the tenant has been executed by the landlord or on the landlord’s behalf.

issues.definition: A tenant’s purchase proceeding remains pending when the price has been deposited but no conveyance has been executed.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s uncompleted purchase proceeding abates when the amended law excludes the religious landlord from the tenant-protection scheme and the amendment takes effect before conveyance.
material_facts: The landlord was found to be a religious institution within the amended statutory definition.
The tenant’s purchase proceeding had not reached finality when the amendment took effect.
Although the tenant had deposited the price and obtained an order for conveyance, the sale deed was executed only after the amendment took effect.
issues.conclusion: The pending proceeding abated, the tenant’s accrued rights under the purchase scheme ceased to be enforceable, and the later execution of the sale deed was erroneous.
issues.legal_principle: Section 1(3)(f) of the Madras City Tenants’ Protection Act, 1921, as amended by Tamil Nadu Act 2 of 1996, excludes qualifying religious institutions and religious charities from the Act’s protections. Section 3 of the amending Act provides for abatement of covered pending proceedings and cessation of related rights, subject to its proviso for a decree or order executed or satisfied in full before the amendment took effect. The Court noted that the amendment was upheld in N. Sreedharan Nair v. State of Tamil Nadu and approved in Mylapore Club v. State of Tamil Nadu.

rule.if: tenant_land_purchase_proceeding and landlord_is_religious_institution and proceeding_pending_when_exemption_took_effect and conveyance_not_executed

predicates.tenant_land_purchase_proceeding: A tenant is pursuing a proceeding to purchase land from the landlord under a statutory purchase right.
predicates.landlord_is_religious_institution: The landlord is an entity shown to qualify as a religious institution under the applicable definition.
predicates.proceeding_pending_when_exemption_took_e: The tenant’s purchase proceeding had not reached finality when a legal change excluding the landlord from the scheme took effect.
predicates.conveyance_not_executed: No conveyance transferring title to the tenant had been executed when that legal change took effect.

issues.definition: A tenant’s purchase proceeding abates when it is still pending at the time an applicable exclusion for a religious landlord takes effect and title has not yet been conveyed.
